config.title: Build typed denormalization selector

intro.title: Build typed denormalization selector
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a typed denormalization selector function in TypeScript. This function will take a normalized data structure and transform it into a nested, easier-to-use object. You will learn how to use TypeScript's type system to ensure your selector is type-safe, catching errors at compile time. The core concepts involve working with interfaces, generics, and custom type definitions. By the end, you'll have a reusable utility that can handle structured data with full type checking.
intro.usecase: Typed denormalization selectors are essential in data-intensive applications like e-commerce dashboards, where you need to combine product data from multiple normalized API sources into a single, type-safe view. For example, when building an admin panel that displays orders with customer details and product information, selectors efficiently merge these separate data entities while maintaining TypeScript type safety. This pattern prevents runtime errors in complex filtering interfaces, such as when users search through financial transaction records that combine account, user, and payment method data. Developers use typed selectors to create reliable data transformations for real-time analytics dashboards, ensuring UI components receive properly structured, validated data.

objectives: Construct a TypeScript selector function that accepts normalized data structures
Implement denormalization logic to transform nested data relationships
Apply TypeScript generics to create type-safe selector signatures
Configure selector parameters to handle different entity types
Integrate the selector with sample data to verify denormalization behavior
Manipulate type definitions to ensure proper return type inference
Initialize test cases to validate selector functionality with various inputs

steps.title: Import TypeScript types and utilities
steps.instruction: Import the Record type from the TypeScript standard library.
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in Record from 'typescript' or directly from TypeScript's lib.

// Importing a type from TypeScript

steps.title: Define normalized data interfaces
steps.instruction: Define a TypeScript interface named 'User' with properties: 'id' (string), 'name' (string), and 'email' (string).
steps.hint: Use the 'interface' keyword followed by the interface name and property definitions with type annotations.
steps.expectedOutcome: A User interface with typed properties will be created to represent normalized user data.
successCriteria: The User interface is defined with id: string, name: string, and email: string properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the User interface, but make sure all three properties (id, name, email) are included with string types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The User interface isn't properly defined. Check that you're using the 'interface' keyword with the correct property names and types.

steps.title: Define normalized state interface
steps.instruction: Define an interface named NormalizedState that has two properties: users and posts, both typed as Record<string, User> and Record<string, Post> respectively.
steps.hint: Use the interface keyword followed by the interface name, then define properties with their types inside curly braces.
steps.expectedOutcome: A NormalizedState interface is created with typed Record properties for users and posts.
successCriteria: NormalizedState interface exists with users: Record<string, User> and posts: Record<string, Post> properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure both users and posts properties are defined with Record types using the correct interfaces.
steps.feedbackWrong: The NormalizedState interface is missing or doesn't have the correct structure. It should have users and posts properties with Record types.

steps.title: Create sample normalized data
steps.instruction: Create a sampleNormalizedState object that matches the NormalizedState interface. Initialize it with sample data for users and posts.
steps.hint: Define a const variable named sampleNormalizedState and assign it an object with users and posts properties. Use Record types to match the interface.
steps.expectedOutcome: A sampleNormalizedState object is created with typed sample data that matches the NormalizedState interface structure.
successCriteria: sampleNormalizedState is defined as a const variable with users and posts properties containing sample records that match the User and Post interfaces.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure sampleNormalizedState has both users and posts properties with Record<string, User> and Record<string, Post> types.
steps.feedbackWrong: The sampleNormalizedState object doesn't match the expected structure. It should have users and posts properties with records of User and Post objects.

steps.title: Define denormalized result interface
steps.instruction: Define an interface named DenormalizedPost that includes a Post object and a full User object for the author.
steps.hint: Create a new interface with properties for the post and author. Use the existing Post and User interfaces as types.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a DenormalizedPost interface ready to represent the output of your selector.
successCriteria: The DenormalizedPost interface is defined with a post property of type Post and an author property of type User.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure your interface includes both a post (Post type) and an author (User type).
steps.feedbackWrong: The interface is not defined correctly. It should have properties for the post and author with proper types.

steps.title: Create the denormalization selector function signature
steps.instruction: Create a function named denormalizePost that takes a postId string and a NormalizedState as parameters, and returns a DenormalizedPost or undefined.
steps.hint: Define the function with explicit TypeScript parameter and return types using the interfaces you created earlier.
steps.expectedOutcome: A typed function signature for denormalizePost that will serve as the foundation for implementing the selector logic.
successCriteria: The denormalizePost function is defined with correct parameter types (string, NormalizedState) and return type (DenormalizedPost | undefined).
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function has both parameters with correct types and the proper return type annotation.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function signature doesn't match the expected types. Review the parameter and return type requirements.

steps.title: Implement the denormalization logic
steps.instruction: Inside the denormalizePost function, implement the logic to look up the user by authorId from the state and return a combined DenormalizedPost object.
steps.hint: Access the user from state.users using the post's authorId as the key. If the user exists, return a new object with post properties and the user. If not found, you can return null or handle the missing case appropriately.
steps.expectedOutcome: The denormalizePost function now contains the core logic to look up and combine user data with post data.
successCriteria: The denormalizePost function body includes: 1) retrieving the post from state.posts, 2) looking up the user by authorId from state.users, 3) returning a DenormalizedPost object with combined data or null if not found.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but the implementation might be incomplete. Make sure to handle both the post lookup and user lookup, and return the proper DenormalizedPost object.
steps.feedbackWrong: The denormalization logic isn't implemented correctly. Review how to access nested properties in the state and combine them into the expected return type.
